name: Data sharing / clean room
description: Two organizations analyze joint data without either handing the other a copy: the provider publishes governed, live shares (no files, no pipelines — consumers query the provider's data in place), sensitive collaborations run inside a clean room where each party's raw rows stay invisible and only approved query templates over the intersection may run (aggregate-only outputs, minimum group sizes, no row-level exfiltration), and whatever leaves the room passes a governed egress gate with audit. The pattern replaced the SFTP-and-CSV era's twin failures — stale copies and unbounded liability once data left your hands — with access that is live, revocable, and provably constrained. There is deliberately no landing or copy layer: the pattern's value is collaboration without moving or duplicating raw data.
when_to_use: Choose this for partner and customer data delivery (data-as-a-product), retail-media and advertising measurement (matching audiences without exposing customer lists), and any regulated collaboration where lawyers would never sign off on shipping raw rows.
Sharing works best when both parties are on, or can reach, the same platform ecosystem; clean rooms specifically earn their complexity when the join itself is the sensitive act.
Partners will only collaborate if raw data never leaves their control.
when_not_to_use: Inside one organization, this is overkill — internal governance (18) and a catalog do the job.
If the partner genuinely needs a copy to ingest into their own stack, honest file/API delivery beats a share they will just export from.
Clean rooms also cannot conjure trust from nothing: without agreed match keys, query approval processes, and legal frameworks, the technology is an empty room.

hot_spots.title: Query templates
hot_spots.detail: Overly broad templates leak more than partners agreed to share.

hot_spots.title: Threshold gaming
hot_spots.detail: Repeated small queries can reconstruct individual-level data.

hot_spots.title: Governance drift
hot_spots.detail: Shares outliving their agreements become silent compliance debt.

stages.name: Provider shares
stages.role: Publish live, governed, revocable access to selected datasets without copying
stages.rationale: Snowflake Secure Data Sharing is the most mature implementation of zero-copy sharing — provider grants, consumer queries, revocation is instant, and reader accounts cover partners without their own Snowflake; its Marketplace extends the same rails to commercial distribution. Delta Sharing is the open-protocol counterweight (hence delta-lake here): REST-based, consumer-platform-agnostic, the right choice when partners are not on your vendor — with Databricks providing the managed experience. BigQuery Analytics Hub is the GCP-native equivalent; Iceberg-based sharing via REST catalogs is emerging for lakehouse estates. The strategic question is ecosystem: same-platform partners make vendor sharing frictionless, heterogeneous partners push you toward open protocols.

stages.name: Clean-room joins
stages.role: Privacy-constrained collaboration: joins over the intersection with raw rows invisible to both sides — dedicated clean-room vendors (Habu/LiveRamp, Samooha pre-acquisition) lack corpus entries; platform-native rooms are the recommendation
stages.rationale: The platform-native route is now the default: Snowflake Data Clean Rooms (the Samooha acquisition, no separate slug) put provider-defined query templates, join policies, and aggregation constraints directly on the sharing rails, so a room is configuration rather than new infrastructure — Databricks Clean Rooms and BigQuery's Data Clean Rooms are the same move on their platforms. Independent vendors (LiveRamp/Habu, Decentriq — none in the corpus) still matter for multi-platform advertising ecosystems and identity-graph matching. The design work is not the tool but the constraint set: which templates may run, minimum aggregate sizes, noise where warranted, and crucially the match-key strategy — hashed emails and identity-provider keys determine match rates, and match rates determine whether the collaboration is worth anything.

stages.name: Governed egress
stages.role: Control and audit what leaves: aggregate-only results, approved destinations, full lineage of released outputs
stages.rationale: Egress is where clean-room guarantees survive or die — results that exit must be aggregate-bounded, destinations enumerated, and every release attributable. The platforms enforce the in-room constraints, but cross-cutting policy and audit benefit from a governance layer: Immuta for policy-driven control over which derived outputs may land where, Satori for uniform monitoring of who pulled what, DataHub/OpenLineage to keep lineage from shared source to released aggregate queryable when a partner (or regulator) asks. Operationally, treat every egress path as a product decision with an owner — the room's contract is only as strong as its least-reviewed export.
